questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Output order before the call
questions.learningObjective: trace print statements that run before the recursive call

options.misconception: believes the print statement runs after the recursive call returns
believes the base case also prints the argument it was handed
believes the guard fires one step early so the first call never prints

questions.explanation: Each frame prints before it hands control to the level below, so the numbers appear while the stack is still growing. Only the deepest call returns, and at that point every frame that could still print has already printed, so the chain unrolls in silence. That is why a statement placed above the recursive call reads the arguments from largest to smallest, with no need to unroll anything.
questions.hint: Ask whether the print runs on the way down or on the way back up.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Output order after the call
questions.learningObjective: trace print statements that run after the recursive call

options.misconception: believes the print runs before the call is made, not after it returns
believes the base case also prints the zero it was handed
believes the stopping test is the value one, so the top level never prints

questions.explanation: The descent happens first and prints nothing, so the program stays silent until the base case is reached. Unwinding begins there, and the pending print statements fire from the deepest frame upward, which is why the smallest argument appears first. Nothing in the body can print before the call returns, so the order of the arguments is inverted relative to the version that prints on the way down.
questions.hint: Ask which frame gets control back first after the chain ends.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Work before and after the call
questions.learningObjective: combine pre-call and post-call work in one printed order

options.misconception: believes the returning half of the body also reports outermost first
believes both halves of the body wait until the deepest call returns
believes the negation changes the argument instead of the printed value

questions.explanation: The first half of the body prints on the way down, so it produces the levels in descending order. The second half can only run after the level below has returned, and the frame closest to the base case is the first one to regain control, so the smallest level is negated and printed first. Reading the two halves as one descending list and one ascending list is the trap: the returning half is ordered by how quickly frames unroll, not by the size of the argument.
questions.hint: Split the body in two and treat each half separately.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Call-tree shape with two recursive calls
questions.learningObjective: read the printed order of a call tree that forks in the body

options.misconception: believes the label is written only after both halves have been walked
believes each half ends by writing its own label a second time
believes the top label is written again on the way back

questions.explanation: A body with two recursive calls forks, so the tree at depth three holds fifteen calls rather than three. The label is written before the fork, so each of the seven calls that gets past the guard writes its own argument, and the eight calls that land on the guard return in silence without writing anything. Each label therefore appears twice except the one at the top, and the order follows the rule of finishing a whole half of the tree before starting the other.
questions.hint: Count the calls that get past the guard before you count the output.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Accumulator seeding
questions.learningObjective: predict the return value of a sum carried in an accumulator

options.misconception: believes the seed is only padding and the run always starts at zero
believes the chain still reaches five because the stop is at zero
believes the accumulator only changes on the last step before the stop

questions.explanation: The accumulator is the running total, and it is already one when the first call begins, so every argument the chain folds in is added on top of that starting value. The descent visits four, three, two and one, then stops and hands back the accumulator, which now holds one plus all four of them. Treating the seed as decorative is the trap: it is not a stand-in but the value the entire chain accumulates onto, so changing it changes the answer by exactly its own amount.
questions.hint: Write down the accumulator after each call, not just the argument.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Accumulator with multiplication
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a product accumulator from a sum accumulator

options.misconception: believes the accumulator adds the levels together rather than multiplying
believes the chain still reaches six because the stop is at zero
believes the accumulator starts at zero and can never leave it

questions.explanation: Multiplication by a product accumulator folds five, four, three, two and one into a value that starts at one, and a run that starts at one is the neutral element for this operation. The neutral element differs from the one a sum needs, which is why the same accumulator shape is safe for a sum and silently wrong for a product. A seed of zero would look like a real total but would erase the answer on the very first step.
questions.hint: Ask which value leaves a running product unchanged when it multiplies it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Accumulator holding a running minimum
questions.learningObjective: seed a minimum accumulator so the extreme value survives

options.misconception: believes the accumulator is set by the first element and never compared again
believes the helper keeps the largest measurement and reports that
believes the seed value passes straight through and is what comes back

questions.explanation: Each level folds the current measurement into the running best by taking the smaller of the two, so the value that survives is the smallest over the whole prefix that has been scanned. The seed has to be something no measurement can beat, which is why the largest possible value is used here; a seed taken from the data would be fine too but a seed of zero would cap every positive measurement at zero. The final level returns the accumulator unchanged because the index has reached the length.
questions.hint: Ask what the seed must be for the running best to stay honest.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Accumulator holding a running maximum
questions.learningObjective: choose a seed that survives an all-negative input

options.misconception: believes a seed of zero is harmless because zero is neutral for maximum
believes the first element is reported directly instead of being compared
believes the accumulator keeps the smallest reading and returns that

questions.explanation: The running maximum has to start below every reading it might meet, and a seed of zero is above all three of these, so every comparison would keep the zero and the answer would be a number that is not in the array. Using the smallest possible value instead lets the readings displace the seed one at a time, and the last one to be greater than everything before it is the one that survives. Zero is a safe seed for a sum of nonnegative values, which is why it is such a common wrong choice here.
questions.hint: Ask whether any of the readings could ever beat a seed of zero.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Reversal by post-call concatenation
questions.learningObjective: reverse a string by appending the first character after the recursive call

options.text: tac
cat
options.misconception: believes the first character is placed in front so the order never changes

options.text: act
options.misconception: believes each level swaps the leading pair exactly once

options.text: tca
options.misconception: believes the first character is moved to the end only at the top level

questions.explanation: Each level recurses on everything except the first character, so the call below it has already reversed the tail of the string, and this level then puts the character it held in front of that reversed tail. The last character of the input is the first one the deepest call sees, so it lands leftmost and the original first character lands rightmost. Writing the character in front of the recursive call instead would rebuild the input in its original order, which is the mistake this shape invites.
questions.hint: Ask which character the deepest call is handed and where it ends up.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Reversal by accumulator direction
questions.learningObjective: reverse a string by prepending each character to an accumulator

options.text: tliuq
quilt
options.misconception: believes the new character is appended behind the accumulator

options.text: tliu
options.misconception: believes the last character is consumed and never recorded anywhere

options.text: tiluq
options.misconception: believes the final two characters keep their original relative order

questions.explanation: The accumulator travels from level to level, and each level puts its own character in front of what the deeper levels have gathered, so the character read last ends up leftmost. Reading the input left to right therefore deposits the characters in reverse order, and the base case simply hands back the finished text. The same code with the two operands of the plus sign swapped produces the input unchanged, because then the character is deposited behind everything gathered so far.
questions.hint: Ask which character ends up leftmost in the finished string.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Digit building with an accumulator
questions.learningObjective: collect the digits of a number by prepending each peeled digit

options.misconception: believes the peeled digit is appended behind the accumulator
believes the digits are gathered in one left-to-right pass
believes the two most significant digits swap places

questions.explanation: Peeling with division by ten always produces digits right to left, so the accumulator is prepended to on every level: the sevens digit lands first, then the eights digit in front of it, then the zero, and the base case puts the leading nine in front of all of them. The prepending is what undoes the peeling, and the base case has to place its own digit in front of the collected tail rather than just returning it. Appending instead of prepending produces a visibly wrong order, which is the quickest way to catch the mistake.
questions.hint: Write the accumulator after each level and watch which end grows.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Building digits into a mutable buffer
questions.learningObjective: use a StringBuilder so each level appends one digit

options.misconception: believes the append runs before the recursive call
believes the base case runs once more and appends a leading zero
believes the digits are appended on the way down in reading order

questions.explanation: One buffer is shared by every level, and the recursion empties the number down to a single digit before any append happens, so the appends then run from the least significant digit upward. Because each level appends only after its call returns, the digits land in the original left-to-right order without any of them being copied. Moving the append above the call would write the same characters in the opposite order, which is the single most common defect in this shape.
questions.hint: Ask which level reaches the buffer first and which digit it holds.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Recursion over a two-dimensional grid
questions.learningObjective: trace the visit order of a grid fill that marks cells as it goes

options.misconception: believes the open cells are swept in reading order across the grid
believes the wall cell is also marked and reported
believes the upward branch is explored before the sideways branches

questions.explanation: The order is decided by the order of the four calls, not by the shape of the grid: the fill marks a cell, reports it, and only then descends, so each branch is finished before the next one begins. Downward comes first, and that branch alone reaches the bottom half of the map before the upward branch runs out of cells. Seven of the nine cells hold the target value, and the two walls are rejected by the guard, so exactly seven pairs are printed and the last cell printed is the one the upward branch reaches last.
questions.hint: Follow the order of the four recursive calls, not the layout of the grid.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Branch order inside a grid walk
questions.learningObjective: show how the order of two recursive calls changes the visit order

options.misconception: believes the downward call is made before the sideways call
believes the grid is unwound so the later columns are reported last
believes the open cells are reached in column order

questions.explanation: The whole right-hand row is finished before the first downward step, so the top row appears contiguously and only then does the walk start dropping. The eight open cells are all reached because the wall simply blocks one route and the other route around it is still open, and the middle cell of the middle row is the only one that is skipped. Swapping the two calls would produce a completely different list, which shows that the printed order is a property of the body and not of the data.
questions.hint: Ask whether the top row is finished before the walk ever drops a row.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Row-by-row traversal with two indices
questions.learningObjective: print a grid row by row using a column index that wraps

options.misconception: believes the row boundary is detected before the cells are printed
believes only one index moves so the table is read down a column
believes the column index wraps to the next row without a separator

questions.explanation: The column index is what decides whether the body prints a cell or finishes a row, so the first call of a row prints nothing at all and instead spends its time advancing the column until the guard flips. That is why the bar for the first row appears before the second row starts rather than after it, and why one extra bar is printed for the last row before the row index runs off the end. The two indices have to move together for the values to come out in reading order.
questions.hint: Ask when the column guard is true for the first time in each row.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Recursion over a linked structure
questions.learningObjective: trace a linked chain that reports after collecting the rest

options.misconception: believes the report runs before the next node is visited
believes the empty case also reports a stand-in value
believes the nodes are unwound two links at a time

questions.explanation: The report sits below the call that walks to the next node, so the chain is followed all the way to the empty case before anything is printed. From there the frames unroll, and each one reports the value it holds, which is the reverse of the order the nodes were linked in. The returned total comes out correct for the same reason, because each level adds its own value to a subtotal that already covers everything after it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the report can happen before the whole chain has been walked.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Reporting a linked chain in reverse
questions.learningObjective: print a linked chain back to front by recursing before printing

options.misconception: believes the report happens before the call to the next node
believes the head node is never reported because only tails report
believes the head reports last but the rest unwind out of order

questions.explanation: Nothing can be reported until the call to the next node has returned, so the empty case is reached first and the reports then run from the tail node back toward the head. The head frame is the last one to regain control, which is why its value ends up at the end of the output rather than the beginning. This is the simplest way to reverse a linked structure without an accumulator or a second collection.
questions.hint: Ask which node is held by the frame that returns last.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Counting nodes that pass a test
questions.learningObjective: count qualifying nodes by combining a local result with a recursive call

options.misconception: believes every value except the empty marker counts toward the total
believes the chain stops at the first value that fails the test
believes the test is applied to the node value plus the running count

questions.explanation: Every node has to be reached, because the whole chain is walked before any total is final, and each node contributes one or zero depending only on its own value. Four and seven clear the threshold while one and three do not, so the total is the number of nodes plus one, not the number of nodes. The test is applied to the current node, never to the subtotal that is still being built, which is what keeps the result independent of the order the nodes are visited in.
questions.hint: Ask what each node contributes to the total, and to what value the test is applied.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A visited marker on a cyclic structure
questions.learningObjective: stop a walk that can reach a node it has already stood on

options.misconception: believes every link is counted even when it leads back to a visited node
believes the backward link makes the whole walk give up immediately
believes the first node is skipped because nothing points back at it

questions.explanation: The walk counts the nodes it stands on rather than the links it follows, so a node that is entered a second time is recognised by its flag and contributes nothing. One, two and three are each marked once, and the second arrival at two returns immediately, so the total is the number of distinct nodes rather than the number of steps. Without the flag the same walk would keep descending through the same three nodes and the stack would grow until it overflowed.
questions.hint: Ask what happens the second time the walk arrives at the middle node.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Boolean recursion that short-circuits
questions.learningObjective: count the comparisons a boolean search stops at once it succeeds

options.text: 3 times
4 times
options.misconception: believes the exhausted call still runs the body before returning false

options.text: 1 time
options.misconception: believes the array is scanned from the far end toward the front

options.text: 5 times
options.misconception: believes the method keeps descending after it has already answered

questions.explanation: Returning true skips the recursive call in that frame, so no deeper frame is ever created and the elements after the match are never compared. The guard that ends the array is only reached when the search has not found anything, which is why a successful search costs the position of the match and not the length of the array. The count of three matches the fact that the match sits at index two, with the first two elements having failed the test.
questions.hint: Ask how many frames exist once the answer is already known.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Boolean recursion that gives up early
questions.learningObjective: count the comparisons a boolean search stops at once it fails

options.text: 2 times
4 times
options.misconception: believes every entry must be inspected before the method can answer

options.text: 3 times
options.misconception: believes the index starts one place past the front of the array

options.text: 1 time
options.misconception: believes the first entry ends the check including the test itself

questions.explanation: A single offending entry is enough to answer false, so the frame that finds one returns without making the call below it and the remaining entries are never examined. The negative entry sits at index one, so the test runs on the first entry, fails to find a negative, and then runs again on the second and gives up. The guard for the end of the array still exists and would still run if the search reached it, which is why a clean array costs a test per entry while a dirty one costs less.
questions.hint: Ask which entry settles the answer and where it sits.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Counting a mutual recursion
questions.learningObjective: count the entries of a two-method hand-off chain

options.text: 6 times
5 times
options.misconception: believes the call that reaches the stop does not count as an entry

options.text: 11 times
options.misconception: believes each method walks a full copy of the descent on its own

options.text: 7 times
options.misconception: believes the starting call is made twice, once from each method

questions.explanation: The argument is reduced by one on every hand-off, so the chain passes through six values before it reaches the stop, and each of those values costs one entry. The two methods share the chain rather than running one after the other, so the count is the length of the chain and not twice its length. What makes the pair work is that both partners reduce the argument and both stop on the same value, so the chain cannot slip past the stop.
questions.hint: List the argument as it changes at each hand-off.

questions.topic: Printed order under mutual recursion
questions.learningObjective: trace a label that changes with each hand-off between two methods

options.text: d3 u2 d1
d3 u2 d1 u0
options.misconception: believes the stop is the value zero, so zero also prints a label

options.text: u3 d2 u1
options.misconception: believes the first method to be called is the one that prints the letter u

options.text: d3 d2 d1
options.misconception: believes the hand-off between the two methods leaves the label unchanged

questions.explanation: Each method prints its own letter and then hands off, so the letters alternate for as long as the argument is still positive. The label belongs to the method that is entered, not to the method that started the run, so the very first letter is the one the caller named.

questions.topic: Work in the head position
questions.learningObjective: trace a method that reports only after the subtotal exists

options.misconception: believes the report sits in the position before the recursive call
believes the stop also reports before it hands back the value zero
believes the return statement runs between two reports

questions.explanation: The subtotal is captured into a local before anything is reported, which is only possible because the report is placed after the call and the call has already returned by then. From there the reports run outward, so the smallest argument speaks first and the largest speaks last. The value returned is correct for the same reason, since each level adds its own argument to a subtotal that already covers everything below it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Frames live in both call positions
questions.learningObjective: measure the peak number of live frames for a head and a tail shape

options.text: 5 then 5
5 then 1
options.misconception: believes a tail call reuses the caller's frame so the depth never grows

options.text: 6 then 6
options.misconception: believes the stopping frame is also counted as a live frame

options.text: 5 then 4
options.misconception: believes the accumulator shape skips the last step before the stop

questions.explanation: Neither shape escapes the fact that a frame is held from the moment its call is made until the call it made returns, and the language makes no promise that a call in the tail position reuses the frame of its caller. Both bodies therefore reach a depth of one more than the number of non-stopping levels, and the stopping frame never increments the counter because it returns first. The two shapes are equal on this runtime by language rules rather than by accident of the code, so a program cannot rely on the difference.
questions.hint: Ask when a frame is allowed to be released, not whether the call is last.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A loop inside a recursive body
questions.learningObjective: predict output when a bounded loop sits in a recursive body

options.misconception: believes the loop grows as the argument shrinks
believes the stop is the value one, so the last level still runs
believes the stopping frame still draws before it returns

questions.explanation: The loop is bounded by the argument, so each level draws exactly as many digits as its own argument and then a bar to close the frame. Because the loop and the bar both sit above the recursive call, the frames are drawn from the largest argument down to the smallest and never revisited on the way back. The smallest frame is drawn at the argument one, and the call to zero returns before drawing anything, so the last thing printed is that bar.
questions.hint: Ask how many digits the loop runs at the smallest argument that still draws.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A missing stopping rule
questions.learningObjective: recognise the failure produced by a body with no base case

options.text: The call stack overflows and a StackOverflowError is thrown
The method loops forever printing negative numbers without any error
options.misconception: believes a missing base case becomes an endless loop instead of a growing stack

options.text: A NullPointerException is thrown once the argument passes below zero
options.misconception: believes an int that keeps shrinking eventually becomes a null reference

options.text: A StackOverflowError is thrown on the first call before anything is printed
options.misconception: believes the failure is detected before the body has run even once

questions.explanation: Without a guard there is no argument value at which the body declines to call itself, so each call pushes another frame onto the stack and the argument simply keeps falling. The stack has a fixed size set when the thread was created, and asking for more frames than that is answered with an error rather than with an endless loop, because the program is not stuck but out of space. The numbers do print for a long while first, since the failure only happens once the allowance has been used up on the way down.
questions.hint: Ask whether there is any argument for which the body stops calling itself.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A step that moves away from the stop
questions.learningObjective: spot a recursive argument that grows instead of shrinking

options.text: The argument never reaches the guard, so the stack overflows
The method returns 1 because the guard fires on the very first call
options.misconception: believes a base case always fires no matter which way the argument moves

options.text: The method returns 0 because the argument begins above the guard value
options.misconception: believes the guard tests the sign and positive values pass straight through

options.text: The method alternates upwards and downwards and settles on a finite answer
options.misconception: believes there is a hidden second call that reverses the direction

questions.explanation: The guard is a legitimate stopping rule, but the step moves away from it, so the chain sails past zero, then past ten, and keeps going with nothing left to stop it. Termination comes from a measure that strictly shrinks until it matches the stopping value, and here that measure grows, which is the classic way to write a recursion that cannot finish. The result is the same overflow as having no guard at all, and the argument grows large enough to wrap around before the stack runs out.
questions.hint: Ask whether the argument gets closer to the guard value or further from it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: A product accumulator seeded with zero
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an accumulator whose seed destroys the result

options.text: It returns 0 for every input, because the seed is the first factor
It returns 120 for every input, because each level replaces the accumulator
options.misconception: believes the accumulator is overwritten rather than folded into

options.text: It returns 1 for every input, because the last step multiplies by zero
options.misconception: believes the stopping case forces the result to one whatever the seed was

options.text: It returns 5 for every input, because only the first factor survives
options.misconception: believes the recursive step multiplies the argument and discards the accumulator

questions.explanation: A product accumulator has to start at the identity value for multiplication, which is one, and a seed of zero makes every subsequent product zero with no way back. The shape of the code is otherwise correct, which is what makes this defect quiet: it never throws and it never recurses wrongly, it simply reports a value that looks plausible. The same seed is harmless in an additive accumulator, so the habit of reaching for zero carries over and quietly breaks the multiplicative one.
questions.hint: Ask what value leaves a running product unchanged.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: An accumulator joined on the wrong side
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an accumulator that rebuilds the input instead of reversing it

options.text: It returns the input unchanged, because each character is appended behind
It reverses the string, because the accumulator is placed in front
options.misconception: believes the plus sign always keeps the accumulator on the left

options.text: It returns the reversed string with its first character missing
options.misconception: believes the leading character is consumed and never reappears

options.text: It fails with a bounds error once the string has been emptied
options.misconception: believes the stopping case still slices the empty string

questions.explanation: The characters are read left to right and each one is placed behind everything gathered so far, so the accumulator ends up holding them in the order they were read. Only the side of the join decides the direction, which is why swapping the two operands is the whole fix.

questions.learningObjective: explain why a deep recursion fails where a loop does not
questions.stem: A recursive descent through a very long table produces no output at all and the process dies before any row is examined. Explain what is exhausted, and why a loop over the same table succeeds.

options.text: Each live call holds a frame until the call it made returns, and a loop needs only one
Each call reserves a new object on the heap, and a loop reserves nothing at all
options.misconception: believes recursion consumes the heap rather than the call stack

options.text: Each call raises the stack allowance, so a deep recursion needs a larger table
options.misconception: believes the code that recurses is what sets the stack limit

options.text: Each call copies the whole table, so the working set doubles at every level
options.misconception: believes a recursive step duplicates its input by default

questions.explanation: A call holds a frame from the moment it is made until the call it made returns, and that frame carries the parameters, the place to come back to and any local still needed afterwards. questions.topic: What an accumulator buys over combining results

options.text: The result of the call is still needed afterwards, so it is combined with something

options.misconception: believes head position is about output order rather than combining work

options.text: The method owns neither an accumulator nor a stopping case of its own

options.text: The method calls itself exactly once from the first line of its body

That single distinction decides whether a frame has to survive the call, and the stack cost of a recursion follows directly from it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Why the tail position is loop-shaped
questions.learningObjective: relate the tail position to the state a loop keeps in place
questions.stem: A method's only action is to call itself with a smaller argument and hand that call's result straight back. Why is that the shape that maps most directly onto a loop?

options.text: Nothing is done with the result afterwards, so no frame has to hold a value to add
It always runs faster than a loop because no arithmetic is left to do
options.misconception: believes a tail-shaped recursion outruns a loop on raw speed

options.text: It uses less memory because the smaller argument replaces the saved frame
options.misconception: believes the argument value overwrites the frame that was waiting

options.text: It cannot be written as a loop at all, so the two are different in kind
options.misconception: believes recursion and iteration are not interchangeable

questions.explanation: A loop carries its state in variables it updates in place, and nothing has to survive from one iteration to the next because the work of an iteration is finished before the next begins. A call in the tail position is the same idea written in call form, since the value the level below produces is exactly the value this level returns. The shape is called loop-shaped for that reason, even though the runtime still reserves a frame per level unless it is given a reason not to, which is why the stack cost of a deep tail-shaped recursion can still surprise people.
questions.hint: Ask whether anything is left to do once the call returns.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Why a loop survives what a recursion does not
questions.learningObjective: compare the space a loop and a recursion need over the same input
questions.stem: A method recurses once per entry of a very long list and dies partway through, while an ordinary loop over the same list finishes comfortably. What difference matters here?

options.text: Every level holds a frame waiting for a call, and the loop reuses one set of variables
Each level allocates a new object for its entry and the loop allocates nothing
options.misconception: believes heap objects rather than frames are what run out

options.text: Each level copies the whole list while the loop reads the entries in place
options.misconception: believes recursion duplicates its input by default

options.text: The recursion is slower because it cannot use the machine's own arithmetic
options.misconception: believes the cost of recursion is a loss of machine-level speed

questions.explanation: At any one moment a recursion holds a frame for every level that is still waiting, so a descent as long as the list wants a frame per entry, while a loop holds one set of variables because an iteration finishes before the next begins. The allowance for those frames is a fixed size set when the thread is created, so a sufficiently long list exhausts it no matter how much time is available. Choosing between the two forms is therefore partly a question of how deep the recursion would have to go, not only of how it reads.
questions.hint: Ask how many waiting frames the loop needs at any moment.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Where combining work has to sit
questions.learningObjective: place the work that transforms a result on the correct side of the call
questions.stem: A method builds a total and then has to double it before returning. Where does the doubling have to sit for the recursion to work at all?

options.text: After the recursive call returns, because the value to be doubled does not exist yet
Before the recursive call, because the running total is known on entry
options.misconception: believes the total is already complete when the method is entered

options.text: Inside the stopping case, because that is where values are produced
options.misconception: believes only the stopping case ever produces a value

options.text: In the call to itself, because a larger argument is what doubles the result
options.misconception: believes passing a bigger argument doubles the answer

questions.explanation: The total only exists once the levels below have returned their results, so the doubling has to happen on the way back where that value is in hand. Doing it on the way down would transform a number that has not been computed yet, and the same operation would be applied at every level rather than once at the end. This is the practical content of head position: work that combines results cannot be moved to the descent without changing what the method computes.
questions.hint: Ask when the value to be transformed first exists.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: How a grid walk records a visit
questions.learningObjective: state the purpose of the store a grid walk makes before it recurses
questions.stem: A grid walk stores a different value into a cell before it makes any recursive call. What is that store actually for?

options.text: It makes a second arrival at the same cell fall through to the stopping branch
It records how many times the walk has stepped on that cell
options.misconception: believes the stored value is a tally of visits

options.text: It keeps the original cell value so the walk can compare against it later
options.misconception: believes the original value is saved and reused

options.text: It frees the cell so the walk can hand it to the level below
options.misconception: believes the store releases memory for the recursion

questions.explanation: A cell can be reached again from a neighbour, and without some record of that the walk would keep descending through the same cells forever. The store is cheap precisely because the guard that decides whether to recurse is the same test the store invalidates, so the second arrival fails the test and returns instead of forking again. Overwriting is one way to do it and a separate collection of coordinates is another, but the store has to be checked by the guard or it changes nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what the guard would do on a second arrival if the store were absent.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Reading a step-count recurrence
questions.learningObjective: interpret the added unit in a step-count recurrence
questions.stem: A step-count method halves its argument and adds one to whatever the recursive call returns. What does that added one stand for at each level?

options.text: The constant work the level does once, on top of what the level below costs
One whole element of the input that is processed and then discarded
options.misconception: believes the added unit is a whole unit of the data

options.text: One frame that the level keeps alive while the call below returns
options.misconception: believes the added unit is stack space rather than work

options.text: One more level of the tree that a repeated split would have produced
options.misconception: believes the method forks and the added unit is a branch

questions.explanation: A recurrence of the form a smaller cost plus a constant describes a level that pays a fixed price and then waits for the level below, so each added unit is that price paid once per level. Because the argument is halved at every step, the number of levels is the number of halvings rather than the size of the input, which is why such a method stays cheap on data that is enormous. Reading the added unit as a data element, a frame, or a branch each describes a different method than the one that was written.
questions.hint: Ask what the level does that is not part of the call.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Return value against printed output
questions.learningObjective: distinguish when a printed order is produced from when a value is assembled
questions.stem: A recursive method both returns a value and prints as it runs. Why is the printed sequence a separate question from the value that comes back?

options.text: Printing happens in call order while the value is assembled on the way back
Printing also happens on the way back because printing is a statement
options.misconception: believes every statement in a body runs after the call returns

options.text: The value cannot be observed because a method with a side effect returns nothing
options.misconception: believes a method that prints is unable to return anything

options.text: Printing happens first because a return statement is always the final line
options.misconception: believes the last line of a body runs before the rest of it

questions.explanation: The two effects happen at different moments, and which moment depends on where the statement sits relative to the recursive call. A statement above the call runs while the stack is still growing, and a statement below it runs after the level below has returned, so one method can print in the order the calls were made and still return an answer built in the opposite direction. That is why a value can come out correct while the printed sequence is not what a reader expects, and why tracing the two separately is the reliable approach.
questions.hint: Ask which statements sit above the recursive call and which sit below it.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: What a marker changes and what it leaves
questions.learningObjective: separate the effect of a visited marker on extent from its effect on shape
questions.stem: Adding a visited marker to a walk changes how much work it does. What does it change, and what does it leave exactly as it was?

options.text: It bounds the calls by the reachable nodes and leaves the forked body untouched
It turns the walk into a single chain so each node is reached once
options.misconception: believes the marker replaces the branching with a line

options.text: It removes the need for the end-of-structure case in the body
options.misconception: believes the marker replaces the end of the structure

options.text: It cuts the depth of the walk to the length of the shortest route
options.misconception: believes the marker shortens the deepest path

questions.explanation: The marker only turns a second arrival into a case that returns, so the calls it saves are the repeats and the calls it keeps are one per reachable node. The body still forks in the same places and the longest path through the structure is still as long as it was, so a walk that has to stand on every reachable node pays for all of them. The end-of-structure case is untouched as well, since a reachable chain can still end without a backward link, and removing it would break that case.
questions.hint: Ask what the body does differently on the second arrival.

questions.subject: JAVA_PROGRAMMING
questions.topic: Why a stopping case still returns a value
questions.learningObjective: explain the value a base case owes to the level above it
questions.stem: A stopping case sits at the head of every chain, exactly where the combining work sits. Why does it still have to hand a value back?

options.text: The level above combines whatever comes back, so the stopping case owes it a value
A method that returns a value is not allowed to reach the end without one
options.misconception: believes the requirement is about the shape of the method rather than its caller

options.text: The stopping case also has to print the value that it returns
options.misconception: believes returning a value also reports it

options.text: The stopping case has to hand the argument back to the value the caller passed
options.misconception: believes the stopping case returns an argument rather than a result

questions.explanation: The chain does not end with the stopping case as far as its caller is concerned, because the caller is about to add its own piece to whatever arrives. A stopping case that returned nothing would leave the level above with nothing to combine, so it has to supply the value that the combination treats as the identity, which is zero for a sum and one for a product. Choosing that value wrongly is a quiet failure, since the recursion still terminates and still returns a plausible number.
questions.hint: Ask what the level above does with whatever the stopping case returns.
